thread.title: Hungerford: Stocks rack up best quarterly gain since 2013

title: Hungerford: Stocks rack up best quarterly gain since 2013
text:
Save
Wow! U.S. large-cap stocks, as represented by the S&P 500 index, jumped 7.2 percent last quarter, their best three-months results since 2013. If dividends are included, the S&P 500 has reached double-digit gains for this year, posting a solid 10.5 percent rise for the first nine months of 2018.
Both the S&P 500 and the Dow, up 9 percent last quarter, set all-time highs Sept. 22 while small stocks and the NASDAQ reached their record highs Aug. 26. My favorite “cheap” tech stock, Apple (AAPL), up 21.9 percent, led the Dow’s 30 stocks last quarter.
Unfortunately, other stock indices did not perform nearly so well last quarter. Small companies in the Vanguard Small Cap Index fund rose only 4.7 percent, while Vanguard’s Total International fund eked out a mere one-half percent return, hurt by emerging markets that lost 1.8 percent. (Based on p/e ratios, international stocks are about one-fourth cheaper than ours.)
My two favorite investment sectors — technology and health care — continued their terrific performance. Health care surged 14 percent last quarter while tech gained 8.5 percent. My longtime favorite all-purpose health care fund, Fidelity Select Health Care (FSPHX), superbly managed by veteran manager Edward Yoon, has climbed a sensational 26 percent so far this year.
Why has the market done so well? Certainly one reason is investor confidence that reflects the record high business and consumer confidence numbers so ably spelled out by my son Steve in his column here two weeks ago. (See journalnow.com/business , then scroll down to business columnists.)
The number he quoted that impressed me the most was the NFIB Small Business Optimism Index that has been in existence for 45 years. It reached an all-time record high in August! The NFIB survey also reported the best profits ever — no wonder small business owners are so cheerful.
While the widely-watched unemployment rate is at a low 3.9 percent, another unemployment number merits attention. The underemployment rate in August fell to 7.4 percent, its lowest since 2001 and just a little more than half of its 13.7 percent rate from May 2016, 27 months earlier. The underemployment rate represents people working part-time who would like full-time jobs and workers in full-time jobs that are working at jobs far below their skill level (i.e., a college graduate working as a waitress).
Perhaps the key factor driving stock prices higher is the incredible increases in corporate profits. They rocketed 25 percent for the first six months of this year. Companies begin reporting third-quarter profits this week — they are expected to rise a solid 19 percent. An amazing 83 percent of companies exceeded profit estimates for the second quarter, way above the 5-year 70 percent average.
Another positive is that companies are beginning to raise wages, given 690,000 advertised job openings — another record high — that are increasingly hard to fill. Wages grew at an annual rate of 2.9 percent in August, the best 12-month results since 2005. (Amazon announced Oct. 2 that it had hiked its minimum wage to $15 an hour, even for part-time help.)
My big fear three months ago was that an all-out trade war would cause the market to sell off. Certainly China-U.S. trade relations continue to worsen, but because China depends much more on selling products to the U.S. than vice-versa it is under far more pressure to reach an agreement than we are. Chinese stocks are down 15 percent this year while we are up 10 percent — a huge 25 percent difference!
The new MCA (Mexico, Canada, America) trade pact announced Oct. 1 is good news and should help U.S. manufacturers and farmers. General Motors announced that “this agreement is vital to the success of the North American auto industry.” (Since President Trump was elected in November 2016, the economy has added 412,000 new manufacturing jobs through Aug. 31.)
It is impossible to know how trade talks with the Japanese and Europeans are progressing, but certainly the trade rhetoric from the White House has recently become less negative. Beside the possibility of a worsening trade war, the biggest threats to higher stock prices may be higher interest rates and mid-term elections.
The Fed raised interest rates last month and another quarter percent is almost a sure thing at its December meeting. Next year, three more 0.25 percent increases are forecast. However, the interest-rate raises are no surprise and will likely only be implemented if the economy continues to grow 3 percent or more. We grew a terrific 4.2 percent during the second quarter and probably in the mid-3 percent range last quarter. (From 2010 to 2017 average GDP growth was only a lackluster 2.2 percent.)
Politically, the highly-partisan bickering continues. It is expected that the Democrats will capture the House next month, needing to pick up 23 seats. However, most forecasters expect the Republicans to hold on to its narrow edge in the Senate. The Senate races that are now rated the closest are in seven states — Arizona, Florida, Indiana, Missouri, Nevada, North Dakota, and Tennessee. If the Democrats capture complete control of Congress, the market might sell off 5-10 percent.
A little more than a month ago, Aug. 22, the market recorded its 3,453rd calendar day without a 20 percent bear-market downturn. (However, in 2011 it was down 19.4 percent, barely keeping the bear hibernating.) On that day in August, the market was up 325 percent since its nadir March 9, 2009, adding $27.6 trillion to investors’ portfolios since the crash.
Prospects for the fourth quarter, historically each year’s best three months, and next year seem almost too good to be true. No recession is in sight before 2020 at the very earliest. We have not had a down year during the third year of a President’s term since 1939. Those third years have averaged an incredible 17 percent since 1943.
As I review what I have written above, I am worried that my rosy scenario is a much-too-much deep red. Certainly a trade war with the Europeans, oil prices moving up from $80 a barrel to more than a $100, a slowing economy hurt by higher-interest rates, or an impossible-to-predict event could threaten our high-flying stock market.
Still, my not-very-reliable crystal ball is willing to predict the market will be 10-20 percent higher by the time 2019 ends.
